newsitem.title: UK: Army probes guerrilla attack on N. Ireland base.
newsitem.headline: Army probes guerrilla attack on N. Ireland base.

text.p: Military experts sifted through the debris in Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters on Tuesday to determine how suspected Irish Republican guerrillas planted two car bombs inside the base.

Army sources said the bombs, which injured 20 soldiers and 11 civilians, weighed between 500 and 1,000 lbs (250 and 500 kg) each and were planted so that the second exploded near a medical centre where victims of the first blast were being treated.

Security sources said 12 people were still being held in hospital overnight and several were in critical condition from the most serious guerrilla attack in Northern Ireland since twin IRA and Loyalist ceasefires in 1994.

No group claimed responsibility for the attack but politicians, police and army suspected the Irish Republican Army (IRA) or one of its shadowy splinter groups, who are fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland.

Britain's junior Northern Ireland minister appealed to Loyalist guerrillas, who want the province to stay British, not to break their own truce and go on a tit-for-tat cycle of revenge against the 40-percent Catholic community from which Irish Republicans draw support.

"It is a dire challenge to the peace process. There is no doubt that whoever planted these devices was intent on blowing the process which is taking place at the moment out of the water," Michael Ancram told BBC radio.

"The Loyalist paramilitaries have maintained their ceasefire. I believe that this is a trap to try and entice them to drop their ceasefire and I call on them very strongly not to fall into that trap," he said.

Protestant guerrillas have so far held their ceasefire, despite the IRA's return to violence in February with a bomb in London. The ceasefire was rewarded by the inclusion in peace talks of the Loyalists' political representatives, the Progressive Unionist Party and Ulster Democratic Party.

Monday's bomb went off within earshot of a meeting of Loyalist prisoners in the top-security Maze prison to discuss whether or not to maintain their ceasefire. David Ervine of the PUP said he believed Loyalist guerrilla commanders would now meet to consider the truce in the wake of the bomb.
Ervine said the situation was "deep and serious" but urged Protestant guerrillas to hold their truce.
"Do not do what your enemy want you to do," he told Irish radio. "The choices are clear (and) I demand that the choice is for continued retention of the Loyalist ceasefire."
